q: What floor-to-floor height is typical in office building design?
n: About 3.2 meters floor-to-floor is typical, allowing for ceiling clearance plus raised flooring, ductwork, and structural depth, per the source doc.

q: When a developer requires every office space to get natural daylight, what does that do to the floor plate?
o: It stays the same size no matter what
n: Daylight only reaches a limited depth from the exterior wall, so requiring every workstation to be day-lit forces the plan to stay narrow — shrinking the floor plate, per the source doc.

q: Where in an office tower's plan are mechanical, electrical, elevator, and other servicing functions typically grouped?
n: The core is the building's vertical service zone, stacking elevators, stairs, risers, restrooms, and MEP rooms on every floor, per the source doc.

q: Under common building height classification, how many storeys would typically put a structure in the mid-rise range?
n: 10 storeys falls within the mid-rise range (roughly 6-15 storeys) used in Philippine building practice, above low-rise and below high-rise, per the source doc.

q: Which core placement makes it easiest to divide the floor plate into leasable areas?
n: A centered core leaves a uniform ring of usable space wrapping all sides, letting the floor split into tenant areas symmetrically and flexibly, per the source doc.

q: What is a typical office lease-span distance, measured from core/corridor wall to window wall?
n: A lease span of roughly 10-14 meters is the standard planning figure — deep enough for efficient layouts, shallow enough to stay near daylight, per the source doc.

q: Which core placement leaves tenants on the far side with the longest walk to the elevators and exits?
n: With the core along one edge, tenants on the far side must travel a much longer path from elevators/exits, stretching the access corridor, per the source doc.

q: For an office building with about 30,000 sqm leasable across 28 floors, what elevator provision would most likely be planned?
n: Elevator counts scale with both leasable area and floor count — about 1,070 sqm/floor over 28 floors typically needs ~7 passenger cars plus 2 service cars, per the source doc.

q: Given about 30,000 sqm of leasable area across 28 floors, what is the most likely total gross floor area, including non-leasable space?
n: Gross floor area adds a typical 15-20% load factor for core/walls/non-leasable space, bringing 30,000 sqm leasable to about 35,000 sqm gross, per the source doc.

q: Among typical office uses, which one generally needs the biggest floor plate?
n: Trading floors need one continuous, column-light expanse for desks and screens, pushing the floor plate far larger than more subdivided office layouts, per the source doc.
